The Libertarian Case AGAINST Open Borders

If one had to identify the root of discord between libertarians on this topic, it would have to be their differing views on whether public property should be seen as unowned, or the private (albeit diffused) property of domestic tax-paying citizens. [...] The State has completed this homesteading task but was only able to do so by first generating the requisite funds via domestic taxes. Thus, such “public property” belongs to domestic tax paying citizens as they can demonstrate a superior objective link between themselves and the goods in question with respect to foreigners.

[...]

One who agrees this method [of dividing up public property according to taxes paid] is the optimum way to privatize “public goods” in so doing implicitly recognizes that such domestic tax payers have a superior claim to domestic “public property” with respect to foreigners.

This tries to establish a conception of "public goods" for later arguments, so it's not part of the hypothetical scenario, but it still leaves things too loose. I think the right way to view "public property" is as part of a private organization which profited by it through force and fraud. It is not unowned (apparently Block's view), unpatrolled, or owned by tax-payers (apparently Hoppe's view) in any meaningful sense. At best, it's managed by voters, those vocal and mobile enough to poll themselves, rather than those who have direct interest. In ignoring the obvious substance of "public property," the later arguments which rely on its disposition look unsound to me.

In the end, this isn't as much a case against open borders as a case for "public property," in the sense that a group collectively can decide to defend a jurisdiction comprising absolutely-private property. Maybe I'm focusing too much on the minarchist assumptions of the second-best hypothetical, but a case for closed borders would build on property rights and self-ownership, not the opposite.
